correctness.rationale: Exponential-time Brownian displacement has Laplace density with \(\kappa=\sqrt{r/D}\); direct integration over all Voronoi cells gives positive opposite-parity transition \(p(\kappa)\) and mean even-site displacement \(d(\kappa)\). Reflection gives minus \(d(\kappa)\) at an odd site. The finite-state embedded parity chain is irreducible, with exponentially integrable displacements and holding times, so its ergodic reward/time strong law gives the physical velocity; Brownian exponential-killing supremum tails control the incomplete interval. The sign follows from strict monotonicity of \(x\coth x\) and the positive stationary reward denominator. The small-rate coefficient follows by expansions to \(\kappa^2\), and large-rate decay is exponentially bounded. A standalone finite checker reproduced all cell integrals and simulated actual holding-time-conditioned Brownian motion; no infinite assertion is inferred solely from experiments.

originality.rationale: An explicit current sign theorem for a last-reset-site-labeled two-rate Brownian nearest-projection model, with exact formula and small-rate coefficient. Alston–Bertrand have one uniform rate and study self-diffusion; the current is forced to vanish for the common-rate specialization of this geometry. Ghosh et al., Liu et al. and Roberts et al. describe asymmetrically biased potentials or finite-time return phases, not a nearest-site Voronoi projector with rate memory. A generic Markov reward theorem alone does not supply the cell sums and strict hyperbolic-ratio monotonicity. Targeted external and searchable mathematical-record checks yielded no directly dominating same-object statement; residual priority risk remains.

value.rationale: Local resetting to spatial sites models stochastic binding. Allowing binding attempt rates to depend on the last selected sublattice is a physically motivated minimal kinetic asymmetry, distinct from asymmetric potential or biased projection. The exact global zero/positive/negative current classification establishes that geometry and kinetics must both break the relevant symmetry, and excludes scale-driven current reversals. The quadratic rare-reset onset and fast-reset suppression guarantee at least one finite current optimum, providing a nontrivial control-law consequence. This is not merely a generic ergodic theorem or a parameter substitution.
